evidence_summary: Lindsey had represented HD-39 since 1983 and previously chaired the Education Finance and Appropriations Committee.

Meigs was a retired Grissom High School teacher and local Democratic activist but a first-time candidate. Her occupational credibility may have helped, while she lacked the long personal electoral network of the rural incumbents.
Meigs's Total OOF CMO is about +15.1 and her resource-adjusted OOF CMO about +9.7, indicating that modeled campaign resources explain part, but not all, of the residual.

Lewis was a lifelong Madison County resident, local technology-business founder, and the first Black woman to chair the Huntsville/Madison County Chamber of Commerce. Contemporary observers described unusually strong civic standing for a Democratic legislative nominee.

Contemporary reporting said most of Lewis's roughly $95,000 came from individual donors, while most of Butler's much larger total came from PACs. Lewis explicitly presented this as evidence of community support.
Lewis's resource-adjusted OOF CMO remains close to the Total OOF score, so the model's observed resource control does not explain away her positive residual.

Fields was a Cullman County native, Methodist minister, and longtime state employment-service worker who had already won the 98-percent-white district in a 2008 special election. Contemporary voter quotations emphasized that he was regarded as locally embedded rather than socially distant.

The Alabama Republican Party attacked Fields over HB532 as trying to release murderers. Contemporary reporting described the claim as dubious; the bill created a tightly conditioned path to parole consideration for a small class of first-time offenders after at least 20 years. The attack may have reduced Fields's result and makes his positive CMO more notable, but the partisan defense requires caution.

Cheatham had worked for the Alabama Education Association, taught in Morgan County schools for ten years, and led a gubernatorial education-reform committee. These education networks offer a concrete organizational and occupational mechanism separate from general left-right ideology.

Cheatham raised about $87,000 to Collins's $273,000 in the FollowTheMoney summaries. His Total OOF CMO is about +16.7, resource-adjusted CMO +16.0, and fundraising-adjusted CMO +17.7; modeled resources therefore do not explain his positive residual.

Bracy entered the House after six years on the Prichard City Council, including council presidency. The local-office base is a plausible personal-vote mechanism in HD98, although the best surviving biography was published just after election day.

FollowTheMoney summaries report about $100,000 for Bracy versus $12,000 for the Republican. Total OOF CMO is about +20.7 but fundraising-adjusted CMO falls to about +12.9, indicating that resources explain a meaningful minority of the residual.

FollowTheMoney summaries report about $1.14 million for Varner versus $404,000 for Dial. Varner's Total OOF CMO is about +15.5 and fundraising-adjusted CMO about +8.4, so the modeled fundraising advantage explains nearly half of the residual.

Dial had represented the district for years as a Democrat before running as a Republican in 2010. Varner's near tie therefore occurred against an opponent with both long tenure and a preexisting Democratic personal vote, complicating any ideology-based interpretation.

Republican incumbent Jim Preuitt ended his campaign on September 1, roughly two months before the general election, and the party selected businessman Ray Robbins as its replacement on September 7. Fielding therefore faced a late substitute rather than a normally nominated opponent.

Fielding entered the race after a 26-year career as a Talladega County district and circuit judge. This offered unusually broad name recognition and a nonlegislative public-service identity across the district.

The Alabama Police Benevolent Association listed Fielding among its endorsed 2010 candidates after the election. The publication date is post-election, but it confirms support from a law-enforcement organization consistent with his judicial background.
Heath Jones campaigned as a grassroots fiscal and social conservative, opposed Medicaid expansion, advocated term limits, and said he accepted no special-interest money.
The processed state-file feature gives Lindsey a log D:R spending ratio of 3.745 versus -0.765 for Robinson; resource adjustment reduces the pair CMO gap from 35.9 to 30.9 points.
Contemporary campaign material states that Robinson had held HD-23 since 1994.

The production allocation gives HD-53 a -13.65 core statewide margin, while richer unambiguous precinct-link scenarios give -4.38. Including the production regime yields a 9.27-point baseline range and reduces raw overperformance from 69.2 to 61.8 at the scenario mean.
The production finance feature shows a large Democratic spending advantage, but the resource-adjusted OOF score remains above 53 points, so modeled spending explains little of the extreme residual.

HD-53 was approximately 70 percent nonwhite in the project demographics and voted Democratic by 55.6 points legislatively. Its top-ticket and legislative electorates diverged sharply, making coalition turnout and down-ballot voting central alternatives to candidate ideology.
Tommy Hanes was a retired firefighter and commercial fisherman with deep local roots; his campaign emphasized pro-life, pro-family, education, and strong Second Amendment positions.
Daniels's Shor-McCarty score comes from legislative service after the 2014 election and must not be treated as a pre-election voter perception measure.
Drummond's Shor-McCarty score comes from legislative service after the 2014 election and must not be treated as a pre-election voter perception measure.

Betterton had served two terms on the Florence City Board of Education and was in his second City Council term; his long local elected-service record is a strong non-ideological explanation for candidate recognition. WordPress metadata dates the biography to August 12, 2014.

Burkette was a locally raised public-school educator and three-term Montgomery city councilman. Contemporary reporting attributed his special-primary upset partly to his long history as a coach, teacher, and councilman in the district.

The Alabama Democratic Conference endorsed Burkette in the special runoff. Contemporary reporting described the endorsement as shaped by Joe Reed's conflict with John Knight, making organization and intraparty networks a plausible explanation distinct from ideology.

Contemporary reporting documented severe fundraising and campaign-management problems before the special runoff. His later general-election overperformance therefore should not be read as evidence of unusually strong campaign operations.

A later party-switch announcement described Harper's longstanding work in local government, public education, banking, and economic development and credited him with major district job recruitment. These biographical facts support a local-service explanation but are documented retrospectively.

Harper changed from Democratic to Republican affiliation in February 2012, after the scored election. The switch corroborates ideological or constituency fit only weakly: he said his priorities had not changed, while Democratic leader Craig Ford argued that joining the GOP would require substantive voting changes.

Daniels combined a long education-association leadership history with a contemporaneous Alabama Retail PAC endorsement. This cross-institutional coalition is more consistent with pragmatic local credibility than a single left-right campaign identity.

Before running, Drummond had spent decades as a Mobile journalist and as a senior city and county administrator. Her professional network and visibility are plausible non-ideological explanations for her large margin.

Contemporaneous partisan commentary identified White as a lifelong district resident and recently retired adult-education supervisor and explicitly contrasted his local familiarity with his Republican opponent.

Ledbetter had served on the Rainsville City Council and as mayor before his 2010 House campaign. His municipal record supplies a strong personal-vote explanation separate from ideological positioning.

Ledbetter ran as a Democrat in 2010, switched parties before 2014, and then won the same seat as a Republican. A 2013 meeting memorandum reports that he expected most prior Democratic supporters to remain with him, directly suggesting a candidate-centered local vote.
Contemporary reporting placed Beddingfield's total contributions near $60,000 versus roughly $145,000 for Ledbetter. His positive CMO occurred despite a substantial resource disadvantage.

Later official and biographical records identify Breland as the wife of longtime Decatur municipal judge and civic leader David Breland and part of a locally prominent judicial family. This supplies a plausible recognition network, but the evidence is retrospective and does not establish how it affected the campaign.

Figures had represented SD-33 since 1997 after succeeding her late husband, former Senate president pro tempore Michael Figures. Long incumbency and a prominent Mobile political network are major explanations distinct from ideology.
Beasley entered the 2010 Senate contest after multiple terms in the Alabama House, giving him an established legislative identity even though he was not the Senate incumbent.

Beddingfield was president of the Fort Payne City Board of Education by 2008 and still held that office in April 2014. The long, district-relevant school governance role is a strong candidate-recognition mechanism independent of a detailed ideology platform.

Republican Ritchie Whorton entered the general election after defeating an incumbent Republican 58-42 in the primary and publicly emphasized grassroots campaigning, smaller government, and resistance to Montgomery political bosses. Stephens therefore faced an opponent with demonstrated campaign strength and anti-establishment momentum.

McLaughlin represented HD-27 from 2001 through 2010, was born and practiced law in Guntersville, and held extensive local civic memberships. His decade of prior representation gives him a far stronger personal-vote base than a first-time challenger.

Contemporary reporting lists about $13,455 raised by McLaughlin versus roughly $113,956 for Will Ainsworth. McLaughlin's large positive CMO therefore survived an approximately eight-to-one fundraising disadvantage.

FollowTheMoney records only about $5,891 for Heath Jones, while the state-file spending feature shows an overwhelming Democratic advantage. By contrast John Robinson and Tommy Hanes raised roughly $108,569 and $125,109. Opponent resources sharply distinguish the otherwise ideologically similar incumbents.

The Alabama Retail Association endorsed Robinson while AEA records show substantial support as well. His coalition crossed business and education-labor institutions, making a narrow ideological rejection less plausible than opponent and campaign explanations.

FollowTheMoney reports about $85,460 for Drummond against $8,292 for Ralph Carmichael. Louise Alexander's total is unobserved, while Republican Darius Foster raised about $114,147 and ran an intensive community-outreach campaign. The focal candidate had the much easier documented resource matchup.

National Public Radio documented Darius Foster's door-to-door campaign, school-technology and job-fair initiatives, national Republican attention, and success converting at least some prior Democrats. Alexander faced a substantively active opponent rather than a nominal Republican.

Alexander had served on the Bessemer City Council from 1998 through 2010 and held extensive small-business, funeral-home, church, youth, and alumni ties. Her long municipal and community record is a substantial candidate-recognition mechanism.

White faced Dan Williams in both 2010 and 2014, but his OOF CMO moved from about -4.4 to +29.7. A roughly 34-point within-person shift with the opponent held constant is strong evidence that CMO is not a direct ideology measure.

Republican Steve Clouse had represented House District 93 since 1994 and chaired the General Fund Ways and Means Committee. Marsden therefore faced a powerful twenty-year incumbent rather than a typical Republican officeholder.

Clouse publicly favored Medicaid expansion if Alabama's share remained capped at ten percent. Because Marsden also championed expansion, the contest did not present a clean expansion-versus-rejection ideological contrast.

Clouse won about 77.7 percent of the two-party vote in 2010 and 76.7 percent against Marsden in 2014. Marsden essentially matched the prior Democratic nominee's share, weakening any claim that her progressive platform uniquely depressed the Democratic vote.

Morrow had represented HD-18 for 24 years and contemporary reporting tied him to a school-safety law, industrial and road projects, veterans programming, TVA revenue, and direct constituent advocacy. This accumulated personal vote is inseparable from his ideological brand.

Gladden challenged Republican incumbent Becky Nordgren after Nordgren had defeated the prior Democratic incumbent in 2010. The comparison crosses districts with different post-redistricting histories and does not hold opponent incumbency constant.

Means's 2010 defeat followed a federal indictment by roughly one month. After acquittal in two trials, he won a four-way Attalla mayoral race with 69 percent in 2012. The -5.7 to +29.1 CMO change is therefore also a reputation-shock and recovery sequence.

Project finance data show Turner at an extreme spending disadvantage while Means substantially outspent his Republican opponent. Resource adjustment reduces the pair's CMO gap from about 24.7 to 13.2 points.

A complaint publicized one week before Election Day alleged that Turner filed his statement of economic interests late and questioned his ballot eligibility. The contemporaneous report did not establish a final adjudication, so this is campaign context rather than proven misconduct.
